title: Deriving and using P = Fv

learning_outcomes.text: derive P = Fv and use it to solve problems

prior_knowledge_summary: Power is work done or energy transferred per unit time.
Use P = W/t and W = Fs when the displacement is in the direction of the force.
At constant velocity, forces balance along the direction of motion.
For constant velocity, displacement divided by time is velocity.
new_learning: Derive P = Fv from W = Fs and P = W/t.
Interpret P = Fv as the rate at which a force transfers energy while its point of application moves.
Use only the component of force parallel to velocity.
Rearrange P = Fv to find power, force or speed and explain proportional changes.
not_yet_taught: Derivations and calculations for gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.
Variable-force integration or vector dot-product notation.
Engine efficiency calculations as a required method.

visual_planning.reason: Six planned figures distribute the hook, derivation, direction rule, worked use, misconception repair and synthesis. No image assets are created in this four-file package task.

demand_inventory: derive P = Fv from work and power definitions
calculate power from a parallel driving or resistive force and speed
rearrange P = Fv for force or speed
select the force component parallel to motion
combine P = Fv with constant-speed force balance
explain how power changes when force or speed changes
evidence_basis.originality_note: The teaching sequence, contexts and numerical examples are original. Official evidence is used only to identify assessment demand.

blocks.heading: The same push, a different rate
content: Two identical airport trolleys each face a steady 120 N resistive force. One moves at 1.0 m s^-1 and the other at 2.0 m s^-1. The forward force is the same, so why must the faster motor transfer energy twice as quickly?
Predict which trolley needs more power. Then ask what changes in one second: the faster trolley moves twice as far, so the same force does twice as much work in that second.

figure.purpose: Create the need to connect force, speed and energy transferred each second.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper teacher sketch. Show two identical trolleys with equal 120 N forward arrows. In one second the first moves 1.0 m and the second moves 2.0 m. Use sparse coloured path markers and leave the power comparison as a question.
figure.alt_text: Equal forces move two trolleys through different distances in one second.

blocks.heading: Build the formula from ideas you know
content: Definition to remember: power is work done or energy transferred per unit time.
For a constant force in the direction of motion, work done is W = Fs. The controlled formula is P = W/t, so P = Fs/t.
Group displacement divided by time: P = F(s/t). At constant velocity, s/t = v. Therefore P = Fv.
This derivation shows the condition hidden inside the short formula: F is the force component in the direction of velocity.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: work done or energy transferred per unit time

controlled_formulas.name: Work done by a constant force

figure.purpose: Make every substitution in the derivation visible and justified.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper equation flow. Connect W = Fs and P = W/t to P = Fs/t, then circle s/t and replace it with v to reach P = Fv. Annotate that force and velocity are parallel. Use no unexplained extra formulas.
figure.alt_text: An equation flow derives P equals Fv from work done and power.

blocks.heading: Read P = Fv as a one-second story
content: Suppose a conveyor exerts 300 N on boxes moving at 0.80 m s^-1. In one second, the boxes move 0.80 m. The work done in that second is 300 x 0.80 = 240 J, so the power is 240 J per second, or 240 W.

The short calculation P = Fv = 300 x 0.80 = 240 W says exactly the same thing. Force tells us the energy transferred per metre. Speed tells us the metres travelled per second. Their product gives joules per second.
Unit check: N multiplied by m s^-1 gives N m s^-1. Since N m is J, this is J s^-1, which is W.

figure.purpose: Give a physical rate interpretation independent of the symbolic derivation.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper one-second sequence. A conveyor moves a box 0.80 m in 1.0 s under a 300 N force. Show 240 J transferred during the interval and connect it to 240 J per second. Keep labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: A conveyor transfers 240 joules to a box during one second.

blocks.heading: Use the force that acts along the motion
content: A tow rope pulls a boat with force 1.5 kN at 30 degrees to the direction of travel. The boat moves at 4.0 m s^-1. Only the forward component transfers energy into forward motion.
Resolve the useful force first: F_parallel = 1500 cos 30 degrees = 1.30 x 10^3 N.
Now use the formula to remember: P = Fv. Hence P = (1.30 x 10^3)(4.0) = 5.20 x 10^3 W, or 5.2 kW.
Independent check: in 1.0 s the boat moves 4.0 m, so work done in the forward direction is (1.30 x 10^3)(4.0) = 5.20 x 10^3 J. That is 5.20 x 10^3 J s^-1.

figure.purpose: Teach component selection before substitution into P = Fv.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper vector sketch of a boat moving right at 4.0 m s^-1 while a 1.5 kN rope force acts 30 degrees above the forward direction. Resolve the force into a forward component and a perpendicular component. Highlight only the forward component for power.
figure.alt_text: An angled tow force is resolved into components parallel and perpendicular to a boat's velocity.

blocks.heading: A large force does not always mean large power
content: It feels reasonable to say that a larger force always means a larger power. That idea misses the rate at which the point of application moves.

A person holding a heavy suitcase still exerts an upward force, but the suitcase has zero velocity. Its mechanical power from that force is P = Fv = 0. No mechanical work is being done on the stationary suitcase.
The same person lifting the suitcase transfers energy. At a greater upward speed, the same lifting force gives a greater power. The formula links both quantities, not force alone.

A perpendicular force is another warning. If velocity is horizontal and a force is vertical, that force has no component along the motion, so its instantaneous mechanical power for that motion is zero.

figure.purpose: Repair the misconception that force alone determines power.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper comparison table with three cases: heavy suitcase held still, suitcase lifted upward, and trolley moving horizontally under a vertical force. Show force and velocity arrows, then label mechanical power as zero, non-zero, zero without revealing any practice answer.
figure.alt_text: Three force and velocity arrangements show when mechanical power is zero or non-zero.

blocks.heading: Choose the shortest route and check it
content: If force and speed are known, use P = Fv directly. If power and speed are known, use F = P/v. If power and force are known, use v = P/F.
Before substituting, identify the force component along the velocity. At constant speed, first use force balance if the driving force is not stated directly.
Check units every time: W divided by m s^-1 gives N, and W divided by N gives m s^-1.

At fixed speed, doubling the relevant force doubles power. At fixed force, doubling speed doubles power. If either the parallel force component or speed is zero, the mechanical power from that force is zero.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact decision route for direct, inverse and component problems.
figure.brief: Landscape rectangular white-paper decision map. Start with identify force along velocity, then branch to find P, F or v using P = Fv. Add unit checks for W, N and m s^-1 and a small constant-speed force-balance reminder.
figure.alt_text: A decision map selects the relevant force and rearranges P equals Fv.
